title: Introduction to Industrial and Manufacturing Systems Engineering
text:
Welcome
These are the lecture notes for IMSE 111: Introduction to Industrial and Manufacturing Systems Engineering (3 credits) at North Dakota State University. They’re written for first-year students who want to find out what industrial engineering and manufacturing engineering are, where IMEs work, and how they think. They also teach the software skills engineers use every day.
The notes are released one week at a time and will grow into a full textbook.

title: Introduction to Industrial and Manufacturing Systems Engineering
text:
About the course
The NDSU catalog lists the course as IMSE 111. Introduction to Industrial and Manufacturing Systems Engineering. 3 Credits. The description reads:

Overview of industrial engineering and manufacturing engineering professional careers and work environments. Basic skill acquisition using computer software tools to solve engineering problems, prepare reports, plan projects, deliver professional presentations, and manage data. (North Dakota State University, n.d.)

That gives the book two threads. The profession covers what IMEs do, where they do it, and why it matters. The toolkit covers spreadsheets, Python notebooks, project plans, reports, and presentations.

title: 1  What Is Industrial & Manufacturing Engineering?
text:
1.1 Engineering systems, not just things
Most engineering disciplines are named after what they design. Civil engineers design structures, electrical engineers design circuits, and mechanical engineers design machines. Industrial engineers design how everything works together.
The Institute of Industrial and Systems Engineers (IISE) gives the field’s classic definition:
The key word is system. A hospital emergency department, an Amazon fulfillment center, and a combine assembly line are all systems. Each one transforms inputs into outputs through a series of steps, and each can be made safer, faster, cheaper, or more humane. An industrial engineer practices systems thinking, which means asking how a change in one place ripples through the whole system.
Manufacturing engineering is the closely related discipline that focuses on the processes and equipment that physically make products: machining, molding, welding, additive manufacturing, and automation. At NDSU, the two fields share a department because modern production needs both. Someone has to design the process, and someone has to design the system it runs in.

title: 1  What Is Industrial & Manufacturing Engineering?
text:
1.2 Where IMEs work
Because every organization runs on processes, IMEs work almost everywhere:

Manufacturing. Agricultural equipment, aerospace, electronics, food processing, and medical devices.
Healthcare. Reducing patient wait times, scheduling operating rooms, and preventing medication errors.
Logistics and e-commerce. Designing warehouses, routing delivery fleets, and managing inventory.
Service and government. Banks, airlines, theme parks, and public agencies all use IEs to improve service.



 Career spotlight

Industrial engineers by the numbers



According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, industrial engineers held about 365,100 jobs in 2025 and earned a median annual wage of $102,440. Employment is projected to grow 12 percent from 2025 to 2035, much faster than the average for all occupations (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2026).


Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Occupational Outlook Handbook

title: 1  What Is Industrial & Manufacturing Engineering?
section: 1.3 How IMEs think: measure, model, improve
text:
1.3 How IMEs think: measure, model, improve
When an IME looks at a process, a few questions come first:

How much does the system produce per hour? This is its throughput.
How long does each step take? This is its cycle time.
Which step limits the whole system? That step is the bottleneck.
How busy is each resource? This is its utilization.


Worked example: the morning coffee rush
A campus coffee cart has three steps. Each customer is served by one worker at each step.






flowchart LR
  A([Customer<br/>arrives]) --> B[Take order<br/>30 s]
  B --> C[Make drink<br/>75 s]
  C --> D[Pay<br/>20 s]
  D --> E([Customer<br/>leaves])
  style C fill:#ffc82e,stroke:#0a5640,stroke-width:2px




Figure 1.1: Process flow at the campus coffee cart, with the time per customer at each step.





Each step can serve at most \(3600 / \text{time per customer}\) people per hour:



Table 1.2: Capacity of each step





Step
Time per customer
Max customers per hour




Take order
30 s
120


Make drink
75 s
48


Pay
20 s
180






The system can never go faster than its slowest step, so making drinks is the bottleneck and the cart serves at most 48 customers per hour (Table 1.2).
Now suppose 60 customers arrive per hour during the 8 a.m. rush. The takt time, the pace needed to keep up with demand, is
\[
\text{Takt time} = \frac{\text{available time}}{\text{demand}} = \frac{3600 \text{ s}}{60 \text{ customers}} = 60 \text{ s per customer}.
\]
Drink-making takes 75 s, which is longer than the 60 s takt time, so the line keeps growing. If a second barista is added, drinks are finished every 37.5 s on average, and the cart’s capacity becomes \(3600 / 37.5 = 96\) customers per hour. Each barista is then busy
\[
\text{Utilization} = \frac{60 \times 37.5}{3600} = 62.5\% \text{ of the time.}
\]
Find, measure, and relieve the bottleneck, then look for the next one. That habit is the core of the IE approach, and we’ll come back to it with lean in Week 8 and simulation in Week 10.

title: 1  What Is Industrial & Manufacturing Engineering?
text:
1.5 Key takeaways

Industrial engineering designs and improves integrated systems of people, materials, information, equipment, and energy. Manufacturing engineering focuses on how products are made.
IMEs work in nearly every sector: manufacturing, healthcare, logistics, service, and government.
A system’s throughput is limited by its bottleneck. Improving any other step won’t increase output.
Takt time connects the system to customer demand.







TipCheck your understanding






In one sentence, how does industrial engineering differ from mechanical engineering? Mechanical engineering designs machines and devices. Industrial engineering designs the systems (people, equipment, information, materials) those machines operate within.
A process has steps of 40 s, 55 s, and 35 s. What is the bottleneck and the maximum hourly throughput? The 55 s step. \(3600 / 55 \approx 65\) units per hour.
Demand is 80 units in a 4-hour shift. What is the takt time? \(4 \times 3600 / 80 = 180\) s per unit.










NoteKey terms in this chapter






Additive manufacturing — Building parts layer by layer directly from a digital model; commonly called 3D printing.
Automation — Using machines and control systems to perform tasks with reduced human intervention.
Bottleneck — The resource or step with the least capacity relative to demand; it limits the throughput of the entire system.
CNC — Computer numerical control; machine tools whose motions are directed by programmed instructions.
Critical path — The longest sequence of dependent tasks in a project; any delay on it delays project completion.
Cycle time — The time between completions of successive units at a workstation or process; sometimes used for the total time one unit spends in the process.
Gantt chart — A bar chart that shows project tasks against a timeline, including start dates, durations, and dependencies.
Inventory — Stock of materials, work-in-process, or finished goods held to buffer against uncertainty in supply and demand.
Manufacturing engineering — The branch of engineering that plans, designs, and improves the processes, tooling, and equipment used to turn raw materials into finished products.
Motion study — The analysis of the body motions used to perform a task in order to eliminate unnecessary motions and reduce effort, pioneered by Frank and Lillian Gilbreth.
Scientific management — A management approach, associated with Frederick W. Taylor, that uses systematic observation and measurement to find better methods of work.
System — A set of interacting components (people, machines, materials, information) organized to achieve a common purpose.
Systems thinking — An approach that studies how the parts of a system interact and influence the whole, rather than optimizing parts in isolation.
Takt time — The pace of production required to meet customer demand, equal to available working time divided by customer demand.
Therblig — One of the elemental motions (such as search, grasp, transport, and hold) defined by the Gilbreths for analyzing manual work; the word is Gilbreth spelled nearly backward.
Throughput — The rate at which a system produces good output, such as parts per hour or patients per day.
Utilization — The fraction of available time a resource is actually busy, calculated as time used divided by time available.

NoteKey terms in this chapter






Assembly line — A production arrangement in which work moves from station to station in a fixed sequence, with each station adding parts or operations.
Automation — Using machines and control systems to perform tasks with reduced human intervention.
Industry 4.0 — The fourth industrial revolution, in which connected sensors, data analytics, and automation create smart, adaptive production systems.
Mass production — Making large volumes of standardized products, often on assembly lines, to achieve low unit cost.
Motion study — The analysis of the body motions used to perform a task in order to eliminate unnecessary motions and reduce effort, pioneered by Frank and Lillian Gilbreth.
Scientific management — A management approach, associated with Frederick W. Taylor, that uses systematic observation and measurement to find better methods of work.
Time study — A work measurement technique that times a qualified worker performing a task to establish a standard time.
Toyota Production System — Toyota’s integrated approach to production built on just-in-time flow and jidoka (automation with a human touch); the origin of lean.

NoteKey terms in this chapter






Additive manufacturing — Building parts layer by layer directly from a digital model; commonly called 3D printing.

Capacity — The maximum output a resource or system can produce in a given period under normal conditions.

title: 7  Quality and Statistical Thinking

title: 7  Quality and Statistical Thinking
text:
What quality means to customers
Variation and descriptive statistics
Statistical process control and the control chart
Six Sigma and DMAIC







NoteKey terms in this chapter






Control chart — A time-ordered plot of a process measurement with statistically calculated control limits used to distinguish common-cause from special-cause variation.
Descriptive statistics — Numerical and graphical summaries of data, such as the mean, median, standard deviation, and histogram.
DMAIC — The Six Sigma improvement cycle of Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, and Control.
Quality — The degree to which a product or service meets customer requirements and is free of defects.
Six Sigma — A data-driven improvement methodology that aims to reduce defects to about 3.4 per million opportunities, typically following the DMAIC cycle.
Statistical process control — The use of statistical methods, especially control charts, to monitor a process and detect when it changes.
Variation — The natural differences among outputs of a process; reducing unwanted variation is a central goal of quality engineering.

title: 8  Lean and Continuous Improvement
text: 8.1 Planned topics

title: 8  Lean and Continuous Improvement
text:
Lean manufacturing and the eight wastes (muda)
Value stream maps
5S, kanban, and just-in-time
Kaizen, PDCA, and root cause analysis







NoteKey terms in this chapter






5S — A workplace organization method with five steps, Sort, Set in order, Shine, Standardize, and Sustain.
Just-in-time — A production strategy that makes and delivers exactly what is needed, when it is needed, in the quantity needed.
Kaizen — Japanese for continuous improvement; small, ongoing improvements made by everyone in an organization.
Kanban — A visual signal, often a card or bin, that authorizes production or movement of material only when it is needed downstream.
Lean manufacturing — A philosophy, derived from the Toyota Production System, that maximizes customer value by systematically eliminating waste.
Muda — Japanese for waste; any activity that consumes resources without adding value for the customer.
PDCA — The Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle for iterative improvement, popularized by W. Edwards Deming.
Root cause analysis — A structured method for finding the underlying cause of a problem, using tools such as the 5 Whys and fishbone diagrams.
Value stream map — A diagram of all the material and information flows required to deliver a product, used to identify waste and plan improvements.

NoteKey terms in this chapter






Digital twin — A virtual model of a physical asset or system that is continuously updated with real data to monitor, predict, and optimize performance.
Linear programming — An optimization method in which the objective and all constraints are linear functions of the decision variables.
Operations research — The application of mathematical models, statistics, and algorithms to support better decisions in complex systems.
Optimization — Finding the best decision, such as minimum cost or maximum profit, subject to constraints.
Simulation — Imitating the operation of a real system over time with a computer model to evaluate designs and policies without disrupting the real system.

The Six Sigma improvement cycle of Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, and Control.

title: Appendix B — Glossary
text:
E

Efficiency Profession
How well a process converts inputs into useful outputs, often expressed as actual output divided by standard or expected output.


Engineering economics Profession
The analysis of costs, benefits, and the time value of money to compare engineering alternatives.


Ergonomics Human Factors
The science of designing jobs, tools, and workplaces to fit human capabilities and limitations; also called human factors engineering.

title: Appendix B — Glossary
text:
F

Facility layout Supply Chain
The arrangement of departments, workstations, and equipment within a facility to support efficient flow.

title: Appendix B — Glossary
text:
G

Gantt chart Project Management
A bar chart that shows project tasks against a timeline, including start dates, durations, and dependencies.

title: Appendix B — Glossary
text:
H

Human factors Human Factors
The study of how people interact with systems, used to design work that is safe, comfortable, and resistant to error.

title: Appendix B — Glossary
text:
I

Industrial engineering Profession
The branch of engineering concerned with the design, improvement, and installation of integrated systems of people, materials, information, equipment, and energy.


Industry 4.0 Industry 4.0
The fourth industrial revolution, in which connected sensors, data analytics, and automation create smart, adaptive production systems.


Internet of Things Industry 4.0
Networks of physical devices with sensors and connectivity that collect and exchange data; often abbreviated IoT.


Inventory Supply Chain
Stock of materials, work-in-process, or finished goods held to buffer against uncertainty in supply and demand.

title: Appendix B — Glossary
text:
J

Just-in-time Lean
A production strategy that makes and delivers exactly what is needed, when it is needed, in the quantity needed.

title: Appendix B — Glossary
text:
K

Kaizen Lean
Japanese for continuous improvement; small, ongoing improvements made by everyone in an organization.


Kanban Lean
A visual signal, often a card or bin, that authorizes production or movement of material only when it is needed downstream.

title: Appendix B — Glossary
text:
L

Lead time Operations
The total elapsed time from when an order is placed until it is delivered to the customer.


Lean manufacturing Lean
A philosophy, derived from the Toyota Production System, that maximizes customer value by systematically eliminating waste.


Linear programming Modeling
An optimization method in which the objective and all constraints are linear functions of the decision variables.


Little’s Law Operations
The relationship WIP = throughput × flow time, which holds for any stable system over the long run.


Logistics Supply Chain
Planning and controlling the movement and storage of goods, services, and information from origin to consumption.

title: Appendix B — Glossary
text:
M

Manufacturing engineering Profession
The branch of engineering that plans, designs, and improves the processes, tooling, and equipment used to turn raw materials into finished products.


Mass production History
Making large volumes of standardized products, often on assembly lines, to achieve low unit cost.


Motion study Human Factors
The analysis of the body motions used to perform a task in order to eliminate unnecessary motions and reduce effort, pioneered by Frank and Lillian Gilbreth.


Muda Lean
Japanese for waste; any activity that consumes resources without adding value for the customer.

title: Appendix B — Glossary
text:
O

Operations research Modeling
The application of mathematical models, statistics, and algorithms to support better decisions in complex systems.


Optimization Modeling
Finding the best decision, such as minimum cost or maximum profit, subject to constraints.

title: Appendix B — Glossary
text:
P

PDCA Quality
The Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle for iterative improvement, popularized by W. Edwards Deming.


Process flowchart Operations
A diagram that shows the sequence of steps, decisions, and flows in a process using standard symbols.


Productivity Profession
The ratio of outputs produced to inputs consumed, such as units per labor hour.


Project management Project Management
Applying knowledge, skills, tools, and techniques to plan and execute a temporary effort that creates a unique result.

title: Appendix B — Glossary
text:
Q

Quality Quality
The degree to which a product or service meets customer requirements and is free of defects.

title: Appendix B — Glossary
text:
R

Root cause analysis Quality
A structured method for finding the underlying cause of a problem, using tools such as the 5 Whys and fishbone diagrams.

title: Appendix B — Glossary
text:
S

Scientific management History
A management approach, associated with Frederick W. Taylor, that uses systematic observation and measurement to find better methods of work.


Simulation Modeling
Imitating the operation of a real system over time with a computer model to evaluate designs and policies without disrupting the real system.


Six Sigma Quality
A data-driven improvement methodology that aims to reduce defects to about 3.4 per million opportunities, typically following the DMAIC cycle.


Standard time Human Factors
The time a qualified worker needs to complete a task at a normal pace, including allowances for personal needs, fatigue, and delays.


Statistical process control Quality
The use of statistical methods, especially control charts, to monitor a process and detect when it changes.


Subtractive manufacturing Manufacturing
Making parts by removing material from a solid workpiece, as in milling, turning, and drilling.


Supply chain Supply Chain
The network of organizations, facilities, and flows that sources materials, makes products, and delivers them to customers.


System Profession
A set of interacting components (people, machines, materials, information) organized to achieve a common purpose.


Systems thinking Profession
An approach that studies how the parts of a system interact and influence the whole, rather than optimizing parts in isolation.

title: Appendix B — Glossary
text:
T

Takt time Lean
The pace of production required to meet customer demand, equal to available working time divided by customer demand.


Therblig Human Factors
One of the elemental motions (such as search, grasp, transport, and hold) defined by the Gilbreths for analyzing manual work; the word is Gilbreth spelled nearly backward.


Throughput Operations
The rate at which a system produces good output, such as parts per hour or patients per day.


Time study Human Factors
A work measurement technique that times a qualified worker performing a task to establish a standard time.


Toyota Production System Lean
Toyota’s integrated approach to production built on just-in-time flow and jidoka (automation with a human touch); the origin of lean.

title: Appendix B — Glossary
text:
U

Utilization Operations
The fraction of available time a resource is actually busy, calculated as time used divided by time available.

title: Appendix B — Glossary
text:
V

Value stream map Lean
A diagram of all the material and information flows required to deliver a product, used to identify waste and plan improvements.


Variation Quality
The natural differences among outputs of a process; reducing unwanted variation is a central goal of quality engineering.

title: Appendix B — Glossary
text:
W

Work breakdown structure Project Management
A hierarchical decomposition of a project into smaller, manageable deliverables and tasks.


Work-in-process Operations
Inventory that has started production but is not yet finished; often abbreviated WIP.
